title: Moles, birthmarks and other nevi
intro: A nevus is a harmless collection of skin cells that appears as a mole or birthmark. Most people have between ten and fifty moles, and most are harmless. It is useful to know what normal moles look like and which changes should be checked, because a small number can develop into melanoma.

sections.heading: Common types
paragraphs: Ordinary moles are small, evenly coloured brown spots that appear in childhood and early adulthood. Congenital nevi are present at birth and vary in size. Some people have atypical or dysplastic nevi that are larger and more irregular. Blue nevi are blue-grey, and vascular birthmarks such as port-wine stains and strawberry marks are made of blood vessels, not pigment cells.

sections.heading: How moles change
paragraphs: Moles may darken during adolescence and pregnancy, and many fade or disappear with age. Sun exposure creates more moles. New moles appearing after about age forty need special attention. Having many moles or atypical ones increases melanoma risk, as does a family history.

sections.heading: When to have a mole checked
paragraphs: See a doctor if a mole grows, changes shape or colour, becomes asymmetric, has an irregular border, bleeds, itches, crusts or looks different from your other moles. A new dark spot in adulthood should be checked. Use the ABCDE criteria to guide you.

sections.heading: Examination and removal
paragraphs: A dermatologist can examine moles with a dermatoscope and may take a photograph for comparison. A suspicious mole is surgically removed and examined under the microscope. Moles are not removed just because they are present, but may be removed for cosmetic reasons or if they are repeatedly irritated by clothing. Do not try to remove moles at home.

sections.heading: Birthmarks
paragraphs: Many birthmarks are harmless and fade. Some, such as large congenital nevi, are monitored closely, and some vascular birthmarks can be treated with laser. Discuss concerns with a doctor.

examples.title: Mapping your moles
examples.text: Imagine you have many moles. You could take dated photographs of your back and arms every few months, and compare them for changes or share them with your dermatologist.

examples.title: Asking about a baby's birthmark
examples.text: Suppose your newborn has a red patch on the forehead. You might ask your paediatrician whether it is likely to fade and whether any treatment is needed.
